title: Interlayer dark excitons in a van der Waals heterostructure
authors: Rundong Ma, Konstantin Davydov, Liuxin Gu, Lifu Zhang, Hassan Alnatah, Beini Gao, Ruihao Ni, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Takashi Taniguchi, Kenji Watanabe, You Zhou
abstract: Interlayer excitons in transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures exhibit long lifetimes and long-range transport, making them promising for excitonic devices and quantum many-body phases, such as Bose-Einstein condensates. Achieving these goals requires a precise understanding of spin-allowed bright and nominally spin-forbidden dark excitons, because the lowest-energy exciton species governs population, transport, and condensation. Despite substantial progress, unambiguously distinguishing singlet and triplet interlayer excitons has been challenging, as moiré excitons in these heterostructures can mimic their optical signatures. Here, we report the direct spectroscopic identification of bright (singlet) and dark (triplet) interlayer excitons in high-quality, dual-gated WSe$_2$/hBN/WSe$_2$ homobilayers. Electric-field-dependent photoluminescence and reflectance reveal two momentum-direct interlayer transitions with distinct spin configurations. The interlayer dark excitons obey selection rules that differ from those of bright excitons. Strikingly, interlayer dark excitons retain strong valley polarization, even with their ultralong lifetime exceeding microseconds. Finally, we demonstrate twist-angle control, wherein twist-induced electron-hole momentum mismatch modulates interlayer exciton emission. These results provide critical insights into the electronic and excitonic structure of TMD heterostructures, opening new avenues for excitonic many-body physics and optoelectronic devices.
summary: This work reports the direct spectroscopic identification of bright (singlet) and dark (triplet) interlayer excitons in $	ext{WSe}_2/	ext{hBN}/	ext{WSe}_2$ heterostructures. By using electric-field and time-resolved measurements, the authors confirmed that the dark excitons are long-lived and retain valley polarization. These findings offer critical control mechanisms for excitonic many-body physics and optoelectronic applications.
main_problem: The primary challenge is the unambiguous spectroscopic identification of spin-singlet (bright) versus spin-triplet (dark) interlayer excitons (IXs) in TMD heterostructures, as this spin state dictates population and transport.
main_result: The authors spectroscopically identified two distinct, momentum-direct interlayer transitions ($	ext{IXB}$ and $	ext{IXD}$) with opposite spin configurations, demonstrating that the dark excitons ($	ext{IXD}$) possess ultralong lifetimes and retain strong valley polarization.
method: The study employed electric-field-dependent photoluminescence and reflectance measurements, alongside time-resolved and polarization analyses.
model_or_system: The research uses high-quality, dual-gated $	ext{WSe}_2/	ext{hBN}/	ext{WSe}_2$ homobilayers to study interlayer excitons formed between adjacent TMD layers.
key_observables: Two distinct interlayer transitions ($	ext{IXB}$ and $	ext{IXD}$), opposite circular helicities, ultralong lifetimes (microseconds for $	ext{IXD}$), and field-dependent spectral shifts.
important_parameters: Interlayer splitting ($\sim 19 	ext{ meV}$), electric field strength, and the twist angle between the TMD layers.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed splitting is due to a combination of spin-orbit coupling, binding energy differences, and exchange interaction.
figures_summary: Figures show field-dependent PL revealing both $	ext{IXB}$ and $	ext{IXD}$; reflectance confirms $	ext{IXB}$ absorption but not $	ext{IXD}$ absorption; and TRPL demonstrates the microsecond lifetime of $	ext{IXD}$ compared to $	ext{IXB}$.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the existence of two distinct IX species via field-dependent spectroscopy, then characterizing their differing dynamics (lifetime, polarization) using time-resolved measurements, and finally demonstrating external control over these states using twist-angle modulation.
why_interesting: The ability to spectroscopically separate and characterize spin-forbidden dark excitons alongside their bright counterparts provides fundamental insights into spin-valley locking and exciton dynamics, which are crucial for designing next-generation quantum emitters.

Spintronics.note: The study directly involves the spin state (singlet/triplet) and polarization of excitons in a heterostructure, which is a quantum-optical system relevant to spintronics, particularly concerning spin-related optical transitions.
